MRM-10.title: Purpose, Intended Use and Limitations
MRM-10.one_screen: Development begins by fixing the decision the model is supposed to support, the population and conditions it covers, and the limitations users must respect. Without that mandate, developers cannot choose evidence coherently and validators cannot decide whether "good performance" is relevant to the actual use.

MRM-11.title: Data Lineage and Fitness for Use
MRM-11.one_screen: Model data is not sound merely because it is clean. It must be traceable from source to model, correctly transformed, sufficiently complete, representative of the intended use and governed consistently between development and production; a perfectly coded model trained or run on unsuitable data remains unreliable.

MRM-12.title: Method, Assumptions and Complexity
MRM-12.one_screen: Method selection is a governed judgement about whether the model structure, assumptions and complexity are appropriate for the stated purpose and available data. MRM does not own the derivation of statistical methods; it owns the evidence that the chosen method is defensible, its assumptions are visible, and added complexity earns its place.

MRM-13.title: Implementation, Versioning and Reproducibility
MRM-13.one_screen: A validated methodology is useless if production executes something different. Implementation control proves that approved logic, data transformations, parameters, dependencies and configuration are faithfully reproduced, while versioning and reproducibility make it possible to determine exactly which model generated a past output.

MRM-14.title: Developer Testing and the Pre-Validation Evidence Pack
MRM-14.one_screen: Developer testing is first-line evidence that the model behaves as intended before independent validation begins. It should expose weaknesses rather than manufacture a pass: the pre-validation pack must show what was tested, what failed, what changed, what remains limited and why the developer still believes the model is fit to be challenged for its intended use.

MRM-15.title: Independent Validation: Mandate, Independence and Timing
MRM-15.one_screen: Independent validation asks whether the model is reliable enough for its intended use, what limitations remain, and what controls or corrective actions are required. Independence is substantive, not ceremonial: validators need technical competence, objective incentives, access to evidence and organisational standing to challenge the model owner effectively.

MRM-16.title: The Validation Work Programme
MRM-16.one_screen: A validation work programme turns "independent challenge" into a reproducible examination of the whole model. It asks whether the concept is sound, the data are fit, implementation matches design, performance evidence is persuasive, limitations are understood and actual use stays inside the model's supported boundaries.

MRM-17.title: Outcomes Analysis: Discrimination, Calibration and Backtesting
MRM-17.one_screen: Outcomes analysis asks whether model outputs correspond to real-world outcomes in the way the model's purpose requires. Discrimination tests ranking, calibration tests level accuracy, and backtesting compares prior predictions with realised outcomes; none of them alone establishes that the entire model is sound.

MRM-18.title: Stability, Benchmarking and Challenger Models
MRM-18.one_screen: Stability analysis asks whether the population or model relationships have moved; benchmarking asks whether an independent reference gives a materially different view. These controls catch weaknesses that a model's own historical performance can miss: a stable model can be consistently wrong, and a challenger can reveal a better explanation without automatically becoming the production model.

MRM-19.title: Validation Findings and Issue Disposition
MRM-19.one_screen: Validation evidence must end in a decision-useful opinion, not a pile of tests. Findings translate observed weaknesses into severity, required action, ownership and closure evidence; the validation opinion then states whether the model is fit for intended use, fit only with limitations or not fit, without pretending that validation itself grants approval.

MRM-20.title: Approval and Conditions of Use
MRM-20.one_screen: Approval is the governance act that accepts or rejects residual model risk for a defined use after considering validation, limitations and business need. It can be unconditional, conditional or refused; a conditional approval is a controlled risk decision with explicit restrictions and expiry or remediation, not a way to bypass unresolved validation.

MRM-21.title: Deployment, Use and Overrides
MRM-21.one_screen: A model is not controlled merely because the approved code reaches production. Deployment must reproduce the approved model, users must understand what the output means and where it is limited, and manual overrides must be visible enough to distinguish healthy expert judgement from systematic evidence that the model or its use is failing.

MRM-22.title: Ongoing Monitoring, Thresholds and Escalation
MRM-22.one_screen: Ongoing monitoring asks whether a live model is still performing as expected as products, exposures, customers, data and market conditions change. A monitoring framework is complete only when each signal has an owner, threshold, investigation path and escalation action; a metric dashboard without decisions attached is observation, not control.

MRM-23.one_screen: Model change begins with classification because different interventions solve different problems and reopen different controls. An overlay or adjustment can mitigate a known weakness, recalibration updates levels within an existing structure, and redevelopment changes the model fundamentally; none should become an undocumented production patch.

MRM-24.one_screen: Retirement is a controlled lifecycle transition, not deletion. QNT-01.title: Lending Populations, Samples and Sampling Frames
QNT-01.one_screen: A credit model never learns from "all borrowers". It learns from a sampling frame created by a lender's products, approval rules, geography, data retention and observation period, so the first statistical question is whether the development sample represents the lending population where the model will be used.

QNT-02.title: Credit Labels, Observation Windows and Censoring
QNT-02.one_screen: A binary credit label is not created merely by writing default = 1. The analyst must define an observation start, a performance horizon and what happens to accounts whose outcome is not fully observable; otherwise identical borrowers can receive different labels only because one has been watched longer.

QNT-03.title: Selection, Survivorship and Truncation in Loan Books
QNT-03.one_screen: Loan books are filtered histories, not neutral samples. Approval, payoff, refinancing, sale, write-off, closure and data-retention rules determine which accounts remain visible, so statistical relationships can be distorted even when every surviving record is measured perfectly.

QNT-04.title: Reject Inference
QNT-04.one_screen: A lender observes repayment outcomes for booked applicants but normally not for applicants it rejected. Reject inference addresses this missing-outcome problem, but no statistical technique can recover rejected applicants' true performance without assumptions about how approval relates to risk.

QNT-05.title: Rare Defaults and Class Imbalance
QNT-05.one_screen: Default is often a rare event relative to non-default, especially in high-quality portfolios. That imbalance changes what accuracy means, how much information each event contributes and how unstable estimates become; a model can look excellent by predicting the majority class while learning almost nothing about default.

QNT-06.title: Resampling, Class Weights and Prevalence Correction
QNT-06.one_screen: Resampling and class weighting change how strongly defaults influence model fitting; they do not change the true default prevalence of the lending population. The essential distinction is between altering the training objective to learn rare-event structure and altering the probability scale on which deployed predictions must be interpreted.

QNT-07.title: Vintages, Cohorts and Seasoning
QNT-07.one_screen: Credit performance depends on both calendar time and account age. Vintage analysis fixes the origination cohort so loans are compared at similar seasoning, preventing a new book from appearing safer merely because its borrowers have not yet had enough time to default.

QNT-08.title: Probability Distributions for Credit Events
QNT-08.one_screen: Credit data mix binary events, event counts and positive skewed quantities, so distribution choice must follow the data-generating mechanism rather than convenience. Bernoulli and binomial models describe binary default events under strong independence assumptions; Poisson can approximate rare counts; normal approximations require enough aggregation and weak dependence.

QNT-09.title: Sampling Uncertainty, Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
QNT-09.one_screen: Every observed default rate is an estimate from finite credit history. Standard error measures how much that estimate would vary across repeated comparable samples, while a confidence interval turns that sampling variability into a range generated by a stated procedure; sparse defaults make approximation quality especially important.

QNT-10.title: Hypothesis Tests, p-values, Power and Effect Size
QNT-10.one_screen: A hypothesis test asks whether lending data are sufficiently incompatible with a stated null model to justify rejecting it. The p-value measures extremeness under that null, while power asks whether the test could detect a practically important difference in the first place; neither replaces effect size.

QNT-11.title: Dependence, Correlation and Confounding
QNT-11.one_screen: Credit observations are rarely independent in the everyday sense: borrowers share employers, regions, products and macro conditions, while borrower variables also move together. Correlation measures association, confounding explains how a third factor can create or distort that association, and neither by itself establishes causation.

QNT-12.title: Linear Regression and Its Limits on Binary Outcomes
QNT-12.one_screen: Linear regression makes the statistical predictor concrete: observed outcomes are represented as a linear combination of borrower variables plus a residual, and least squares chooses coefficients that minimize squared residuals. Applied directly to a binary default flag, that machinery exposes its own limits - fitted values can leave the 0-to-1 range and error variance changes with the fitted probability - making a different link function necessary.

QNT-13.title: Logistic Regression and Credit Odds
QNT-13.one_screen: Logistic regression keeps the linear predictor but applies it to log-odds rather than probability itself. This makes fitted default probabilities stay between 0 and 1 while preserving an interpretable coefficient structure; CR owns PD and scorecard construction as credit objects, while QNT owns this statistical estimator.

QNT-14.title: Segmentation and Binning Decisions
QNT-14.one_screen: Segmentation decides which borrowers are statistically similar enough to model together; binning decides which ranges of a predictor are treated as having similar risk. Both trade granularity against statistical stability, and both can manufacture apparent structure when thin lending data are repeatedly partitioned until a pleasing pattern appears.

QNT-15.title: Weight of Evidence and Information Value
QNT-15.one_screen: Weight of Evidence converts each predictor bin into a log ratio comparing where non-defaults and defaults are concentrated; Information Value aggregates those distribution differences across bins. QNT owns these statistical transformations and their failure modes, while CR owns the credit scorecard built from them.

QNT-16.title: Multicollinearity, VIF and Regularisation
QNT-16.one_screen: When lending predictors contain overlapping information, fitted coefficients can become unstable even if overall prediction remains acceptable. VIF quantifies how much linear dependence inflates coefficient variance, while ridge and lasso regularisation deliberately trade some fitting bias for lower variance or simpler models.

QNT-17.title: Decision Trees, Bagging and Random Forests
QNT-17.one_screen: A decision tree learns nonlinear credit rules by recursively splitting borrowers into increasingly homogeneous groups. A single deep tree is high-variance; bagging and random forests answer that weakness by averaging many decorrelated trees trained on resampled observations and subsets of predictors.

QNT-18.title: Gradient Boosting on Credit Data
QNT-18.one_screen: Gradient boosting builds an additive prediction function sequentially: each new shallow tree is chosen to reduce the loss left by the current ensemble. It is powerful on tabular lending data because it captures nonlinearities and interactions, but learning rate, tree complexity and iteration count jointly determine whether it generalises or memorizes.

QNT-19.title: Feature Importance and SHAP Attribution
QNT-19.one_screen: Feature importance asks which variables matter to a model in aggregate; SHAP attribution asks how the fitted model allocated one prediction relative to a baseline. Neither statistic proves causality, and correlated lending variables can make attribution depend strongly on the chosen importance definition and background distribution.

QNT-20.title: Train, Validation, Test and Out-of-Time Design
QNT-20.one_screen: A credit model must be judged on observations that did not participate in fitting or model selection. Training estimates parameters, validation chooses among modelling decisions, final test data estimate performance after those choices, and out-of-time design adds a harder question: does the relationship survive later vintages and economic conditions?

QNT-21.title: Leakage, Overfitting and Generalisation Error
QNT-21.one_screen: A credit model can fail on new borrowers for three different reasons that must not be collapsed into one label: leakage lets the model see information it could not have at decision time, overfitting learns sample-specific noise, and regime change alters the relationship after development. All can create impressive historical results and disappointing deployment, but their remedies differ.

QNT-22.title: Survival Analysis and Time to Default
QNT-22.one_screen: Binary default modelling asks whether an event occurs inside a chosen horizon; survival analysis keeps the timing information and can use accounts whose full future is not yet observed. It separates the probability of surviving beyond a time from the conditional event intensity at that time, making censoring part of the model rather than a reason to discard every incomplete account.

QNT-23.title: Credit Time Series: Stationarity, Trend and Dependence
QNT-23.one_screen: Portfolio default rates, delinquencies and application volumes arrive through time, so nearby observations can share trend, seasonality and serial dependence. Time-series modelling starts by asking whether the process is stable enough for past relationships to repeat; if not, trend, seasonal structure or differencing must be represented before lag relationships are interpreted.

QNT-24.title: Macro Conditioning and Rolling-Origin Forecasts
QNT-24.one_screen: Macro-conditioned credit forecasting links portfolio outcomes to variables such as unemployment, rates or economic growth while respecting the direction of time. IMP owns how forward-looking information enters ECL; QNT owns the statistical lag structure, forecast design and rolling-origin evaluation used to test whether macro relationships genuinely forecast credit outcomes.

QNT-25.title: ROC Curves, AUC and Gini
QNT-25.one_screen: ROC, AUC and Gini measure ranking discrimination, not probability calibration. QNT owns how these statistics are constructed, why AUC has a pairwise ranking interpretation and how prevalence and sample composition affect interpretation; MRM owns thresholds, breaches, escalation and the governance conclusion drawn from the metric.

QNT-26.title: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic in Credit Models
QNT-26.one_screen: The credit-model KS statistic is the maximum vertical separation between the cumulative score distributions of defaults and non-defaults. QNT owns that empirical-distribution mathematics and why KS depends on score ordering, sample mix and finite-event noise; MRM owns any threshold, breach, escalation or remediation attached to the number.

QNT-27.title: Confusion Matrix and Threshold Metrics
QNT-27.one_screen: A ranking model becomes a binary classifier only after a cutoff is chosen. The confusion matrix counts the four resulting outcomes, and sensitivity, specificity, precision and related metrics are different ratios built from those same counts; QNT owns their mathematics, while MRM owns governed thresholds and actions taken when performance breaches occur.

QNT-28.title: Precision-Recall and Discrimination Under Severe Imbalance
QNT-28.one_screen: Precision-recall analysis focuses directly on the rare default class. It is especially informative when defaults are scarce because precision exposes the false-positive burden created by low prevalence, whereas ROC coordinates normalize separately by each actual class and can look strong even when most borrowers flagged as risky do not default.

QNT-29.title: Calibration Curves, O/E, Brier Score and Calibration Tests
QNT-29.one_screen: Calibration asks whether probability levels mean what they say: among loans assigned similar predicted risk, do events occur at roughly that frequency? QNT owns calibration curves, observed-to-expected ratios, probability scoring rules and calibration-test mathematics; MRM owns tolerances, breach classification, escalation and remediation governance.

QNT-30.title: PSI and CSI: Population and Characteristic Drift
QNT-30.one_screen: Population Stability Index and Characteristic Stability Index are bin-based divergence summaries comparing a reference distribution with a later distribution. QNT owns their logarithmic calculation, dependence on binning and statistical limitations; MRM owns monitoring limits, breach escalation and what the institution concludes from a PSI or CSI result.

QNT-31.title: Statistical Comparison of Incumbent and Challenger Models
QNT-31.one_screen: A challenger is statistically meaningful only when compared with the incumbent on the same untouched lending observations, outcomes and horizons. QNT owns paired performance differences, uncertainty around AUC, KS, calibration and loss metrics, and the question of whether an observed improvement is credible beyond sample noise; MRM owns why challengers are commissioned, acceptance criteria, approvals and replacement decisions.

TEC-01.title: Lending Data Grain, Keys, and Row Meaning
TEC-01.one_screen: A lending table is meaningful only when you can say what one row represents. Before writing a join or aggregate, fix the grain, identify the key that should be unique at that grain, and distinguish customer, facility, account, payment, schedule, and snapshot records.

TEC-02.title: Selecting a Reporting Population in SQL
TEC-02.one_screen: A reporting query is first a population definition expressed in code. SELECT chooses the fields, WHERE decides which loan observations enter the analysis, and ORDER BY makes output order deterministic when the order itself matters.

TEC-03.title: Credit Classification with CASE
TEC-03.one_screen: CASE turns an already-defined credit rule into a derived field. It is ideal for delinquency bands, active or closed indicators, exposure bands, and other classifications where mutually understood business conditions must become executable row-level labels.

TEC-04.title: Portfolio Aggregation, Distinct Counts, and HAVING
TEC-04.one_screen: Aggregation changes grain. A loan-level snapshot can become one row per product, vintage, delinquency bucket, or customer segment, but the analyst must choose the grouping columns and the counting unit deliberately or the resulting portfolio measures will answer the wrong question.

TEC-05.title: NULL Semantics in Credit Queries
TEC-05.one_screen: SQL NULL means unknown or missing, not zero, blank, or false. Because comparisons involving NULL usually evaluate to UNKNOWN, missing values can disappear from filters and alter aggregate results without generating any error.

TEC-06.title: Join Cardinality and Exposure Fan-Out
TEC-06.one_screen: A join does not merely add columns; it can change row count and therefore change monetary totals. Before joining loan tables, predict the relationship between the keys on each side and decide whether one input row should match zero, one, or many rows on the other side.

TEC-07.title: Joining Customer, Account, Facility, and Repayment Tables Safely
TEC-07.one_screen: Safe lending joins begin from the table whose grain matches the required output and add attributes only through relationships that preserve that grain. When a child table contains multiple rows per account, aggregate or rank it to the needed grain before attaching it.

TEC-08.title: Month-End Snapshots and Point-in-Time Populations
TEC-08.one_screen: A snapshot table stores repeated observations of the same account through time, so point-in-time analysis requires an explicit observation date. Mixing dates creates a portfolio that never existed and can combine today's balance with last month's delinquency or vice versa.

TEC-09.title: As-Of Joins to Effective-Dated Data
TEC-09.one_screen: An as-of join attaches the version of an attribute that was valid when the loan observation occurred. It prevents future leakage by ensuring an August 2025 snapshot cannot see a customer risk grade assigned in 2026.

TEC-10.title: SQL Date Arithmetic for Reporting Periods, MOB, and Vintage
TEC-10.one_screen: Credit analysis repeatedly converts dates into reporting periods, origination vintages, and months-on-book. The craft is less about memorizing vendor functions than about using explicit boundaries and preserving the distinction between a date, a month label, and elapsed tenure.

TEC-11.title: Window Functions over Loan Histories
TEC-11.one_screen: Window functions calculate across related loan observations without collapsing them into one aggregate row. Their power comes from three choices: which account history forms the partition, how observations are ordered, and which rows are included in the window frame.

TEC-12.title: Delinquency and DPD Sequences in SQL
TEC-12.one_screen: Delinquency analysis is an ordered-history problem: each account observation must be compared with earlier observations at the same grain. SQL windows let the analyst derive prior DPD, roll direction, first delinquency, cure, and consecutive-state behaviour without self-joining the snapshot table repeatedly.

TEC-13.title: First, Latest, and One-Row-per-Loan with ROW_NUMBER
TEC-13.one_screen: Analysts frequently need exactly one record from a repeated history: the latest snapshot, first payment, most recent risk record, or preferred duplicate candidate. ROW_NUMBER makes that choice explicit, but it is safe only when the ordering rule fully determines which row should win.

TEC-14.title: Building Lending Queries with CTEs
TEC-14.one_screen: A common table expression turns a long credit query into named stages whose populations and grains can be inspected. The goal is not to make SQL look elegant; it is to make each transformation explicit enough that duplication, filtering, and aggregate changes can be tested independently.

TEC-15.title: Set Operations and Population Differences
TEC-15.one_screen: Set operations combine or compare compatible query outputs by rows rather than by columns. In credit work they are most useful for stacking like-for-like extracts, finding accounts that appeared or disappeared between populations, and checking whether two keyed sets agree.

TEC-16.title: Writing a Reconciliation Query
TEC-16.one_screen: A reconciliation query implements a comparison that has already been specified: which two populations should agree, at what grain, on which measures, and with what tolerance. TEC owns the executable alignment and exception logic, not the governance decision that defines the control.

TEC-17.title: Implementing Data-Quality Checks in SQL
TEC-17.one_screen: A data-quality rule becomes useful to an analyst only when it can be executed against the real lending grain and return clear exceptions. TEC owns the SQL pattern for checking a supplied rule; DAT owns the governed rule, threshold, severity, and control lifecycle.

TEC-18.title: Query Performance on Large Loan Tables
TEC-18.one_screen: Correct SQL still fails operationally if it scans unnecessary history, multiplies rows, sorts huge intermediate results, or repeats expensive work. Analyst-level tuning starts with reducing data early, preserving useful join keys, and reading the execution plan instead of guessing from query appearance.

TEC-19.title: Loading Portfolio Data into pandas
TEC-19.one_screen: A pandas analysis is only as reliable as the data types and population loaded into memory. Read only the fields and rows required, parse dates deliberately, and check the shape immediately so a five-million-row extract does not become a silent object-typed or memory-heavy mess.

TEC-20.title: DataFrame Grain, Index, and Dtypes
TEC-20.one_screen: A DataFrame is an in-memory table, but its index is not automatically a business key and its dtypes are not cosmetic. Credit analysis remains safe only when the analyst separately tracks row grain, key uniqueness, index behaviour, and the storage type of each important field.

TEC-21.title: Filtering and Assigning Credit Data in pandas
TEC-21.one_screen: pandas filtering is the in-memory equivalent of defining a SQL population, while assignment adds derived lending fields to that population. The safe pattern is to build explicit boolean masks, select with .loc, and avoid chained operations whose target is ambiguous.

TEC-22.title: Missing Data and Nullable Types in pandas
TEC-22.one_screen: Missing data in pandas can appear as NaN, NaT, None, or pd.NA depending on dtype. The analyst's job is not to make missing values disappear; it is to detect them consistently and decide whether to preserve, flag, fill, or exclude them without changing the credit meaning.

TEC-23.title: Portfolio Aggregation with pandas GroupBy
TEC-23.one_screen: groupby changes a loan-level DataFrame into a portfolio summary at a chosen grouping grain. As in SQL, the hard part is not the syntax: it is deciding whether the metric counts rows, accounts, facilities, customers, or non-missing observations and making that choice visible.

TEC-24.title: Merging DataFrames Without Multiplying Exposures
TEC-24.one_screen: A pandas merge has the same cardinality risk as a SQL join: duplicated keys on the right can multiply balances on the left. pandas adds a valuable defence through merge validation, which lets the analyst state the expected relationship and fail immediately when the data violates it.

TEC-25.title: Point-in-Time Matching in pandas
TEC-25.one_screen: Point-in-time matching in pandas attaches the latest attribute known on or before each loan observation. merge_asof is designed for this ordered problem, but it requires sorted keys and a clear direction so a historical row never matches a future risk record.

TEC-26.title: Reporting Dates, MOB, and Vintage Cohorts in pandas
TEC-26.one_screen: pandas date operations should preserve the same lending meanings used in SQL: reporting period is the observation period, vintage is the origination cohort, and months-on-book is elapsed calendar tenure. Converting dates once and working with periods avoids fragile string slicing and approximate day arithmetic.

TEC-27.title: Delinquency Sequences with GroupBy, Shift, and Rolling Operations
TEC-27.one_screen: Longitudinal credit work in pandas depends on sorting each account history correctly and then using grouped operations that never cross account boundaries. shift, cumulative calculations, and rolling windows reproduce many SQL window patterns while keeping one row per account observation.

TEC-28.title: Reshaping Portfolios into Vintage and Migration Views
TEC-28.one_screen: Credit portfolios often need to move between long account-history data and compact cohort or migration matrices. Reshaping is safe only after the analyst knows the source grain and whether duplicate combinations should be impossible, aggregated, or counted.

TEC-29.title: Vectorized Credit Calculations
TEC-29.one_screen: Portfolio calculations should usually operate on whole pandas Series or NumPy arrays rather than one Python row at a time. Vectorization is faster, easier to test, and clearer when the rule can be expressed as column arithmetic, boolean masks, grouped transforms, or array selection.

TEC-30.title: Assertions, Testing, and Reproducible Analyst Outputs
TEC-30.one_screen: A finished credit analysis is not just a DataFrame or query result; it is a rerunnable transformation with executable evidence that the population, grain, dates, and controlled totals remained correct. Assertions make silent analytical assumptions fail loudly before the output is exported or consumed downstream.

TLM-01.title: Treasury as the balance-sheet control centre
TLM-01.one_screen: Bank treasury is the control centre for the consequences created by the whole balance sheet: funding, liquidity, structural interest-rate risk, structural foreign exchange, collateral and the internal price of balance-sheet resources. Customer businesses originate assets and liabilities; treasury makes the combined result fundable, liquid and inside risk appetite.

TLM-02.title: From accounting balance sheet to ALM map
TLM-02.one_screen: ALM stops reading the balance sheet as accounting labels and starts reading it as dated cash flows, repricing events, currencies, rate bases and options. Assets can equal liabilities plus equity exactly while the bank remains heavily mismatched in time, rate and currency.

TLM-03.title: The behavioural balance sheet: the model is the assumptions
TLM-03.one_screen: For most treasury numbers, the contractual schedule is only an input; the usable balance sheet is created by behavioural assumptions. Non-maturity deposit persistence, deposit beta and lag, loan prepayment and committed-line drawdown determine the cash flows that feed IRRBB, liquidity stress and FTP: the model is the assumption set.

TLM-04.title: How a solvent bank runs out of cash
TLM-04.one_screen: FND-05 → solvency asks whether value and loss-absorbing resources cover obligations; liquidity asks whether cash is available when payment is due. A bank can be economically solvent and still fail because valuable assets cannot be converted into the required cash, currency or settlement balance fast enough without unacceptable loss.

TLM-05.title: The banking-book perimeter
TLM-05.one_screen: The banking-book/trading-book boundary determines which prudential risk machinery applies; it is not shorthand for “held long term” versus “traded often”. Interest-rate sensitivity exists economically on either side, but structural ALM and IRRBB focus on banking-book positions while foreign-exchange capital rules can reach currency positions across the bank.

TLM-06.title: Where IRRBB comes from
TLM-06.one_screen: IRRBB is one structural risk with several mechanisms: repricing mismatch, yield-curve shape, basis and optionality. Closing one mechanism does not close the others, so an apparently “matched” banking book can still move materially in earnings or economic value.

TLM-07.title: One rate shock, two objects: NII and EVE
TLM-07.one_screen: FND-04 → NII is interest income minus interest expense; FND-08/09 → present value changes when discount rates or expected cash flows change. IRRBB hits two different objects: near-term earnings and the economic value of future banking-book cash flows, and the two measures can move in opposite directions because they use different horizons and cash-flow assumptions.

TLM-08.title: Repricing gaps and time buckets
TLM-08.one_screen: Repricing gap analysis puts rate-sensitive assets and liabilities into the period of their next effective reset, then shows where timing mismatch sits. It is a diagnostic map of gap risk, not a complete NII forecast and not a liquidity ladder.

TLM-09.title: Duration, present-value sensitivity and its limits
TLM-09.one_screen: Duration compresses a stream of cash flows into a first-order estimate of value sensitivity to yield changes. It is useful EVE intuition, but a bank balance sheet cannot be reduced safely to one duration gap when curves move non-parallel, bases differ and behavioural cash flows change with the scenario.

TLM-10.title: Non-maturity deposits: balance life, beta and lag
TLM-10.one_screen: A non-maturity deposit can be legally withdrawable now yet behave as persistent funding whose administered rate reprices slowly. ALM must model two separate objects—balance persistence and rate response—because a stable balance can still be highly rate-sensitive, and a sticky rate does not prove the balance will remain.

TLM-11.title: Prepayment, early redemption and behavioural optionality
TLM-11.one_screen: Customer options make banking-book cash flows conditional on incentives rather than fixed by contract. Borrowers can shorten assets through prepayment, depositors can shorten liabilities through early redemption, and the option is most valuable to the customer when exercising it is least convenient for the bank.

TLM-12.title: Pipeline and commitment behaviour
TLM-12.one_screen: Not every treasury exposure is already funded on the balance sheet. Fixed-rate origination pipelines can create interest-rate exposure before drawdown, while committed but undrawn facilities create contingent liquidity because the customer controls whether and when cash is demanded.

TLM-13.title: IRRBB scenarios, limits and supervisory outliers
TLM-13.one_screen: IRRBB stress asks how one balance sheet behaves under severe rate paths and changed behaviour, then compares ΔNII and ΔEVE with appetite and supervisory screens. A supervisory outlier threshold is a trigger for attention, not a target and not proof that exposure just below it is safe.

TLM-14.title: Hedging structural interest-rate risk
TLM-14.one_screen: A hedge changes the bank’s exposure only if its sensitivity offsets the risk being managed; matching derivative notional is not enough. ALM hedging therefore aligns tenor, curve point, benchmark, optionality and scenario behaviour, then checks both NII and EVE because reducing one can worsen the other.

TLM-15.title: Structural foreign exchange in the banking book
TLM-15.one_screen: Structural FX is the banking-book problem created when assets, liabilities, capital interests and funding needs sit in different currencies. A bank can hedge spot FX value yet remain dependent on FX-swap markets for funding, and it can hold ample aggregate liquidity while being unable to deliver the currency that must settle.

TLM-16.title: Funding liquidity versus market liquidity
TLM-16.one_screen: Funding liquidity risk is the risk that the bank cannot obtain the cash it owes on time without unacceptable loss; market liquidity risk is the risk that an asset cannot be sold or financed quickly near its expected value. Funding stress can force asset sales, and poor market liquidity can turn those sales into losses that worsen the funding run.

TLM-17.title: The liquidity inventory: cash, HQLA and monetisable assets
TLM-17.one_screen: A liquidity buffer is not the nominal value of “safe securities”; it is the cash value of assets that are eligible, unencumbered, operationally available and monetisable in the required currency under stress. HQLA is the regulatory LCR subset; internal counterbalancing capacity may be broader but must reflect real execution constraints.

TLM-18.title: Cash-flow ladders and liquidity gaps
TLM-18.one_screen: A liquidity ladder places expected cash inflows and outflows into the periods in which cash must actually move, then shows discrete and cumulative funding gaps. Unlike a repricing gap, it cares about settlement cash; unlike LCR, it can use institution-specific buckets and behavioural assumptions across horizons longer or shorter than 30 days.

TLM-19.title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
TLM-19.one_screen: LCR asks whether recognised HQLA can cover standardised net stressed cash outflows over 30 calendar days. It uses regulatory runoff, drawdown and inflow assumptions; it is not a forecast of the next month and not a linear survival clock.

TLM-20.title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio
TLM-20.one_screen: NSFR asks whether the bank’s asset and off-balance-sheet profile is supported by sufficiently stable funding over a one-year structural horizon. LCR protects against a short stress using a liquid-asset stock; NSFR constrains the funding structure that can create excessive dependence on short-term refinancing.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Net Stable Funding Ratio — Available and required stable funding*, Basel Framework NSF30, consolidated framework.
Reserve Bank of India, *Basel III Framework on Liquidity Standards – Net Stable Funding Ratio*, RBI/2020-21/95, DOR.No.LRG.BC.40/21.04.098/2020-21, 5 February 2021; effective 1 October 2021.
European Parliament and Council, *Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 on prudential requirements for credit institutions and investment firms*, Part Six, consolidated version current as at 1 January 2026.

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Net Stable Funding Ratio: Liquidity Risk Measurement Standards and Disclosure Requirements — Final Rule*, 20 October 2020; effective 1 July 2021.
Prudential Regulation Authority, *Modernising the liquidity policy framework*, CP5/26, March 2026.

TLM-21.title: Liquidity stress testing and survival horizon
TLM-21.one_screen: Internal liquidity stress testing replaces normal behavioural and market assumptions with severe but plausible ones, then follows the bank’s cash position through time. Survival horizon is the first point at which credible usable resources no longer cover required cash; it is scenario-specific and is not implied by LCR or NSFR.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.

European Banking Authority, *Guidelines on ICAAP and ILAAP information collected for SREP purposes*, EBA/GL/2016/10, 3 November 2016; applicable from 1 January 2017.

TLM-22.title: Intraday liquidity and payment timing
TLM-22.one_screen: A bank can end the day with enough cash and still fail during the day because payments are time-specific. Intraday liquidity is the capacity to meet payment and settlement obligations when they must settle, including in the right currency, before offsetting receipts arrive.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Monitoring tools for intraday liquidity management*, BCBS 248, 11 April 2013.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.

TLM-23.title: Collateral, encumbrance and secured funding capacity
TLM-23.one_screen: Collateral converts asset value into borrowing capacity, but only after eligibility, haircut, legal availability and operational timing are recognised. Encumbrance is the record of liquidity already spoken for: the more assets pledged to existing transactions or margin needs, the less optionality treasury has when stress arrives.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Monitoring tools for intraday liquidity management*, BCBS 248, 11 April 2013.

TLM-24.title: Contingency funding and liquidity crisis execution
TLM-24.one_screen: A contingency funding plan turns stress analysis into an executable crisis playbook: triggers, decision rights, funding actions, collateral, communication and escalation. “Sell securities” or “use the central bank” is not a plan unless amount, currency, haircut, timing, documentation, ownership and operational readiness are known.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.
Reserve Bank of India, *Guidelines on Liquidity Risk Management, Liquidity Risk Monitoring Tools and LCR Disclosure Standards*, DBOD.BP.BC.No.56/21.04.098/2012-13, 7 November 2012.
Prudential Regulation Authority, *The PRA’s approach to supervising liquidity and funding risks*, SS24/15, January 2026; effective 20 January 2026.

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, *Regulation YY — Enhanced Prudential Standards for Bank Holding Companies and Foreign Banking Organizations*, 12 CFR 252.34(f), as amended 1 November 2019.
European Banking Authority, *Guidelines on ICAAP and ILAAP information collected for SREP purposes*, EBA/GL/2016/10, 3 November 2016; applicable from 1 January 2017.

TLM-25.title: Funding strategy, maturity concentration and rollover risk
TLM-25.one_screen: Funding strategy determines which liabilities support the asset base before stress begins: source, tenor, currency, instrument and counterparty concentration all shape resilience. The central danger is rollover dependence—assets remain outstanding while funding reaches maturity and must be replaced at a price or in a market the bank does not control.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.
Reserve Bank of India, *Guidelines on Liquidity Risk Management, Liquidity Risk Monitoring Tools and LCR Disclosure Standards*, DBOD.BP.BC.No.56/21.04.098/2012-13, 7 November 2012.

TLM-26.title: What FTP transfers — and what bad FTP creates
TLM-26.one_screen: Funds transfer pricing gives business lines an internal price for the funding and contingent-liquidity consequences they create, while treasury manages those risks centrally. It is also a behavioural control: if FTP is flat, stale or incomplete, rational businesses will originate the wrong assets, gather the wrong deposits or sell commitments whose hidden balance-sheet cost sits in treasury.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, SR 16-3, 1 March 2016.

TLM-27.title: Matched-maturity FTP and the transfer curve
TLM-27.one_screen: Matched-maturity FTP prices an exposure against the internal cost or value of funding with a comparable effective tenor rather than against one average funding rate. The transfer curve should represent marginal balance-sheet economics: what the next unit of funding or stable funding value costs now, not what historical liabilities happened to cost.

sources.label: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, SR 16-3, 1 March 2016.
Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10, December 2011.

TLM-28.title: FTP for behavioural and contingent products
TLM-28.one_screen: Behavioural products cannot be priced correctly from legal maturity alone. NMD FTP needs a governed replication of stable balances and repricing behaviour; prepayable assets need effective tenor that changes with expected exercise; commitments need a charge for standby liquidity even before cash is drawn.

sources.label: Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10, December 2011.

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, SR 16-3, 1 March 2016.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31, updated 16 July 2024, effective 1 January 2026.

TLM-29.title: ALCO, risk appetite and the treasury control loop
TLM-29.one_screen: ALCO is where the bank turns measurements into balance-sheet decisions: what mismatch to retain, which limit to tighten, what to fund, hedge, reprice or stop originating. FND-18/19 → risk appetite and policy hierarchy set the boundaries; treasury produces the integrated view, while independent risk challenges whether assumptions, limits and actions actually control the exposure.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144, 25 September 2008.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31, updated 16 July 2024, effective 1 January 2026.
Reserve Bank of India, *Guidelines on Liquidity Risk Management, Liquidity Risk Monitoring Tools and LCR Disclosure Standards*, DBOD.BP.BC.No.56/21.04.098/2012-13, 7 November 2012.

TLM-30.title: One balance sheet, four regulatory implementations
TLM-30.one_screen: Mechanics stay common across borders; deltas sit in scope, calibration, reporting, supervisory process and dates. As at August 2026, RBI’s 2025 IRRBB framework is issued but not yet effective.
